extracted.intended_audience: teachers, educators, and students of education or cognitive psychology
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for developing and assessing meanings, conceptions, and understanding in learners — how meanings are acquired, defined, and used, and how instruction should move from concrete to abstract. Focuses on clarity, types of definition, and the active nature of concept formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning as the central aim of thinking
rubrics_metrics.description: To find out what facts mean... is the object of all discovery; to find out what facts will carry out, substantiate, support a given meaning, is the object of all testing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructional or scientific activity should explicitly seek to elicit, clarify, and test meanings; inference and judgment are applications and growths of meanings. A successful inference attains a goal of meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence of meaning and understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: To grasp a meaning, to understand, to identify a thing in a situation in which it is important, are thus equivalent terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a learner does not grasp the meaning (e.g., does not understand a word or event), there is no intellectual object for thought. Teaching should ensure that students identify meanings, not merely sense impressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish direct and indirect understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct understanding: grasping meaning at once (apprehension). Indirect understanding: roundabout, mediated grasping requiring search (comprehension).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design tasks that recognize both modes: build directly apprehensible meanings through experience, but also train students in mediated inference for unfamiliar cases. Recognize that learning presupposes some existing meaning while exposing blind spots that prompt reflection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build a store of portable meanings
rubrics_metrics.description: Our power to think effectively depends upon possession of a capital fund of meanings which may be applied when desired.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Curriculum should develop a repertoire of concepts students can apply to new situations; ensure transferability by practicing application across contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acquire definiteness and consistency of meaning through activity
rubrics_metrics.description: The problem of the acquisition of meaning... is the problem of introducing (i) definiteness and distinction and (ii) consistency or stability of meaning into what is otherwise vague and wavering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use practical, hands-on activities (rolling, bouncing, using tools) that elicit distinctive responses tied to particular qualities so learners form stable, distinct conceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification by use and function rather than merely sensory traits
rubrics_metrics.description: Variations in form, size, color... have much less to do, and the uses, purposes, and functions of things and of their parts much more to do, with distinctness of character and meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize functional/contextual features in teaching distinctions (e.g., tool use) rather than relying only on perceptual differences that learners may not notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceptions serve as instruments: identification, supplementation, systematization
rubrics_metrics.description: Conceptions... are instruments (i) of identification, (ii) of supplementation, and (iii) of placing in a system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate concepts by whether they help identify particulars, supply plausible supplementary attributes for incomplete observations, and integrate observations into broader conceptual systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concept formation is an active, iterative process
rubrics_metrics.description: The child... tries to apply to every new experience whatever from his old experience will help him understand it, and as this process of constant assumption and experimentation is fulfilled and refuted by results, his conceptions get body and clearness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor learning designs that require hypothesis, testing, revision of concepts (trial and error, corrective feedback) rather than passive accumulation of examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceptions are general by application, not by residue-extraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Conceptions are general because of their use and application, not because of their ingredients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess generality of student concepts by their applicability to new cases rather than by listing shared features abstracted from multiple exemplars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid vague, gelatinous meanings; strive for perspicuity
rubrics_metrics.description: A constant source of misunderstanding and mistake is indefiniteness of meaning... Vagueness disguises the unconscious mixing together of different meanings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require clear, single, self-contained statements of meaning (intension); use definition and classification exercises to reduce ambiguity. Encourage sincerity and vigor in seeking precision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use definition (intension) and division/classification (extension) together
rubrics_metrics.description: Intension is meaning as a principle of identifying particulars; extension is the group of particulars identified and distinguished... Taken together, definition and division put us in possession of individualized or definite meanings and indicate to what group of objects meanings refer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When teaching a concept, provide both a clear defining principle and examples/non-examples (classification) to specify its extension. Evaluate whether the definition successfully marks off target cases from close alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ denotative, expository, and scientific definitions appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions are of three types, denotative, expository, scientific... the first and third are logically important, while the expository type is socially and pedagogically important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use denotative (direct experience) definitions to ground sense qualities; use expository definitions (illustrations, dictionary accounts) as pedagogic intermediates; adopt scientific (causal/genetic) definitions to explain why objects have their properties and to increase applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer causal/genetic (scientific) definitions for deeper understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific definitions select conditions of causation, production, and generation as their characteristic material... this scientific definition is founded... on the way in which certain things are causally related to other things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach concepts by explaining relations and causal mechanisms (e.g., why whales are mammals) to provide transferable, explanatory power rather than merely descriptive lists of traits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure familiarity is built from active responses and repeated use
rubrics_metrics.description: Familiar acquaintance with meanings thus signifies that we have acquired in the presence of objects definite attitudes of response which lead us, without reflection, to anticipate certain possible consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design repeated, purposeful tasks that create consistent anticipatory responses in learners (habitual responses tied to meaning) so terms become directly apprehensible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious of overreliance on expository/bookish substitution
rubrics_metrics.description: There is danger that instead of inciting one to effort after personal experiences that will exemplify and verify them, they (expository definitions) will be accepted on authority as substitutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require verification through experience or active inquiry rather than letting students accept secondhand definitions uncritically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret the concrete-to-abstract maxim correctly
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete denotes a meaning definitely marked off... The maxim 'to proceed from the concrete to the abstract' means starting from meanings that are definite and familiar, not from mere sensory objects without thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin instruction with concrete meanings that are already directly apprehensible for the learner, then guide translation to more abstract, mediated concepts; avoid presenting sensory activities devoid of reflective interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test definitions by their discriminatory power
rubrics_metrics.description: The test of the distinctness of a meaning is that it shall successfully mark off a group of things that exemplify the meaning from other groups, especially of those objects that convey nearly allied meanings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate definitions by their ability to include target cases (extension) and exclude close non-targets; use counterexamples and near-miss cases in assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use systematization to increase scientific power
rubrics_metrics.description: Science consists in grouping facts so that general laws or conclusions may be drawn from them... scientific notions make explicit the systematizing tendency involved in all use of concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether taught concepts fit into broader systematic relations (laws, classifications) that allow derivation and prediction; encourage students to connect particulars to systemic frameworks.
